title: Given the head of a linked list that contains a cycle, return the node where the cycle begins. If there is no cycle, return null. Solve it with constant extra space. (LeetCode: Linked List Cycle II)
shortTitle: Start of LinkedList Cycle (Finding the Loop Entry Node)
keyPoints: Phase 1 uses Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves one step, fast moves two steps; if they meet, a cycle exists.
Phase 2 resets one pointer to the head, then both advance one step at a time; they meet at the cycle's entry node.
The correctness relies on the distance relationship: the fast pointer travels exactly twice the slow pointer's distance.
If no cycle exists, the fast pointer reaches null and the method returns null.
Both phases together run in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
A common mistake is advancing at double speed in phase 2; both pointers must move at equal single-step speed.

s1_definition.oneliner: After the pointers meet in the loop, send one back to the head and walk both one step at a time; they meet at the loop's start.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Phase 1 (detection)** – slow moves one node, fast moves two nodes per step; if they meet, a cycle exists.
- **Phase 2 (entry finding)** – reset one pointer to the head, advance both at one step; they meet at the cycle's entry.
- **Distance proof** – fast traveled 2x slow's distance; algebra shows head-to-entry distance equals meeting-point-to-entry distance around the loop.
- **No cycle** – if fast reaches null, return null.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh confirmed that a chain of transaction records at National Bank of India loops back on itself, and now he needs the exact record where the loop rejoins the chain to fix the corrupted pointer. After the fast and slow readers meet inside the loop, he moves one reader back to the start of the chain and walks both forward at the same pace. Where they meet again is precisely the corrupted record.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  head → T1 → T2 → T3 → T4 → T5
                    ↑              │
                    └──────────────┘
                    (cycle: T5 → T3)

  Phase 1: slow and fast meet inside the loop (say at T4)

  Phase 2:
    entry = head (T1)    slow = T4 (meeting point)
    T1 → T2              T4 → T5
    T2 → T3              T5 → T3
         ↑ MEET!              ↑ MEET!

  Both meet at T3 = cycle entry
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the node where a linked list cycle begins is a two-phase extension of Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm, running in linear time with constant extra space. Phase 1 is ordinary cycle detection: slow moves one step, fast moves two. If they meet, a cycle exists. If fast reaches null, there is no cycle.

Phase 2 uses a distance relationship. Because fast traveled exactly twice slow's distance, algebra shows that the distance from the head to the cycle entry equals the distance from the meeting point around the loop back to the entry. So resetting one pointer to the head and advancing both at equal single-step speed makes them converge at the entry node.

The single detail people get wrong is the speed in phase 2. Both pointers must move at equal single-step speed, not at the original 2:1 ratio. The 2:1 ratio is only for phase 1 to create the distance equation. Phase 2 relies on equal-speed stepping to converge at the entry.

In a banking repair tool at National Bank of India, the integrity checker detected a loop in a transaction chain, and the repair tool needed the exact record where the loop started to reset the corrupted next pointer. The extended Floyd algorithm found it using only pointers, no extra memory.

Remember one sentence: after the fast and slow pointers meet, reset one to the head and walk both at equal speed; they meet at the cycle's entry.
